questions: Is each candidate family recognisable as one clinical area?
Where a family has no dominant NHS classification, is there a real clinical grouping the metadata does not capture?
Where two families overlap strongly, are they one area or two?
For the most widely shared features: one clinical concept, several concepts sharing wording, or an artefact of how pathways were written?
Should paediatric pathways be separate families, variants within families, or handled by every family?
Is trauma one family, several anatomical families, or a dimension that cuts across families?
Is there any pair of families that must not be separated, because a clinically critical route runs between them?
clinical_review.review_pack_note: A per-family review document is generated alongside this report. It lists representative pathways, dominant classifications and the specific questions being asked about each family.

conclusion.next_question: Do the benefits of these smaller networks justify the runtime, governance and coordinationcomplexity compared with a monolithic model?
paragraphs: Multiple independent methods produce repeatable candidate groupings, and the presented set contains 34 candidate families. That is sufficient evidence to carry a federated or hierarchical architecture forward into Phase 3 for comparison with amonolithic alternative.

The families are not independent clinical islands. About 63% of pathways cross a proposed family boundary, 424 features are shared broadly across families, and 22% of pathways remain highly ambiguous on structural evidence alone.

Any viable federated design would therefore need to handle cross-family reasoning andshared evidence, potentially through shared or hierarchical structures, rather than simplyrunning completely isolated Bayesian Networks. The proposed family boundaries still requireclinical review before they can be treated as model boundaries.
conclusion.title: Federated families are credible candidates, but their boundaries are porous

configuration.note: Every threshold and weight used by Phase 2 is configurable and is listed here. None is clinically validated; they are stated so the evidence can be reproduced or re-run differently.

does_not_tell_us: Whether a federated design is preferable to a single model. Phase 2 shows where boundaries could be drawn, not whether they should be.

structural.agreement_note: Agreement is measured on a scale where 1.0 means the two methods produced the same grouping and 0.0 means no more agreement than chance.
structural.description: Which pathways hand over to each other most. Several clustering methods were run independently, so agreement between them is itself evidence rather than one algorithm's opinion.
structural.label: Connection structure

executive_summary.bottom_line: Federation is credible enough to compare in Phase 3, but any viable federated designmust account for cross-family reasoning, shared evidence and clinical validation.
executive_summary.headline: Repeatable candidate families emerge, but they are not independent islands.
key_points: The presented candidate set contains 34 families; the typical family contains 7 pathways and the largest contains 123.
About 63% of pathways cross a proposed family boundary, showing that the families remain strongly connected to one another.
424 features are shared broadly across candidate families, so a separated design would need to decide what is shared and what is duplicated.
22% of pathways remain highly ambiguous on structural evidence alone, and all proposed family boundaries still require clinical review.
executive_summary.summary: Phase 2 tested existing NHS groupings, graph structure and shared clinical featuresindependently and in combination. The results provide enough evidence to carry a federated or hierarchical option into Phase 3, but not enough to treat the proposedfamilies as final clinical boundaries.

metric_tooltips.boundary_pathway_count: Pathways in this family that hand over to, or receive handovers from, a pathway in a different family.
metric_tooltips.clinical_areas: The clinical areas most of this family's pathways are listed under. Pathways can belong to several areas, so these are the most common rather than the only ones.
metric_tooltips.cohesion: A plain summary of how well the family holds together on two independent measures: how much its pathways hand over to each other, and how much clinical vocabulary they share. 'High' means both agree; 'low' means neither is strong. It says nothing about whether the family is clinically correct.
metric_tooltips.cross_family_hub_count: Pathways that connect several other families at once and sit on many of the routes through the estate. A structural description, not a clinical judgement.
metric_tooltips.external_link_percentage: The remainder: handovers that cross into another family.
metric_tooltips.internal_link_percentage: Of all the handovers leaving this family's pathways, the share that stay inside the family. Higher means the family is more self-contained. Shown as 'not measurable' where the family's pathways have no handovers at all.
metric_tooltips.name_basis: Where the family's name came from. A family is only named after an NHS classification when one value covers at least half its pathways; otherwise it keeps a neutral name, because inventing a clinical-sounding name would imply a claim the evidence does not support.
metric_tooltips.overlapping_families: Other candidate families this one shares a substantial amount of clinical vocabulary with. Overlap is a prompt for review, not a reason to combine them.
metric_tooltips.pathway_count: How many pathways this candidate family contains. A pathway is one clinical assessment flow.
metric_tooltips.shared_core_dependencies: How many of this family's features are also used by several other families. These are the things that would need either sharing or duplicating if the families were separated.
metric_tooltips.symptom_groups: The NHS symptom groups most common among this family's pathways.
metric_tooltips.unique_discriminators: Distinct symptom discriminators reachable from this family. Discriminators are the clinical factors that separate more urgent presentations from less urgent ones.
metric_tooltips.unique_dispositions: Distinct outcomes this family can reach, such as an ambulance response or a referral within a stated time.
metric_tooltips.unique_questions: Distinct questions the family's pathways can ask between them. The same question can be used by several pathways and is counted once.
metric_tooltips.unique_snomed: Distinct SNOMED clinical concepts recorded against answers in this family. SNOMED coverage in this dataset is sparse, so this is a partial view.

merge_candidates.mechanical_caveat: Combining two families always increases the share of handovers that stay inside the result, because handovers that used to cross the boundary now sit within it. That measure therefore cannot tell a good merge from a pointless one. The measure that can is clinical similarity, which falls when a merge combines pathways that connect to each other without being clinically alike.

meta.confidentiality: Contains derived NHS Pathways analysis. Handle according to programme information governance requirements.

evidence_classes.candidate: A possible grouping, boundary or shared structure suggested by the evidence. Requires clinical review and architectural judgement before it means anything.
evidence_classes.derived: Calculated from measured values using a stated definition. The definition is given with the figure.
evidence_classes.measured: Counted directly in the NHS Pathways dataset.

meta.question: If federation were chosen, what candidate Bayesian families might exist?
meta.scope_note: This report presents measured and derived evidence only. It makes no architectural recommendation: comparing monolithic against federated designs is Phase 3 work.
meta.title: Discovering Candidate Bayesian Families

methodology.definition: A group of pathways that the evidence suggests could form one Bayesian model. Produced by an algorithm or an existing classification, and not clinically confirmed.
One method of proposing families. NHS classifications, connection clustering and combined-similarity clustering were run independently, so that agreement between them is evidence in itself.

A handover between two pathways in the same family is internal; one crossing into another family is external. The internal percentage is internal divided by internal plus external, counted over the handovers leaving a family's pathways.

Feature similarity is the proportion of the combined feature set that both sides share, from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical). It takes no account of set size, so two very small families can score 1.0 from a handful of shared items; the tables therefore carry the family sizes alongside.

Fewer than 200 distinct outcomes exist and most families can reach a similar subset, so outcome similarity is high for almost every pair and cannot distinguish them. It is measured and reported, but the low/moderate/high banding uses questions, discriminators and SNOMED concepts only.
methodology.term: Why outcomes are excluded from the overlap banding

methodology.definition: Measured as the adjusted Rand index: 1.0 means two methods produced the same grouping, 0.0 means agreement no better than chance. It ignores how the groups are labelled or how many there are.

The family set shown in the explorer is 'hybrid_a', chosen in configuration because it requires both connection evidence and clinical-feature support before keeping a group. That is a modelling choice, not a finding that it is the right family set; all strategies are compared.

A family is named after an NHS classification only when one value covers at least 0.5 of its pathways. Otherwise it keeps a neutral name, because inventing a clinical-sounding name would imply a clinical claim the evidence does not support.

criteria: Cost to run, including cost per assessment
next_phase.description: Phase 3 will take the candidate structures from this phase and compare three ways of building a Bayesian model, measuring each against the same criteria.

Which pathways belong to which family, including overlaps
The shared features and how much duplication they imply
The boundary pathways and features that would need coordinating
The merge and split alternatives, to size a range rather than one option

options.detail: One Bayesian Network covering the whole estate, following the existing Pathways structure directly.
options.label: Single model, as the data is written

options.detail: One Bayesian Network where questions meaning the same thing are represented once rather than repeated.
options.label: Single model, clinically normalised

options.detail: Several smaller Bayesian Networks based on the candidate families from this phase, with shared structure where needed.
options.label: Federated or hierarchical models

overlap.interpretation_note: High overlap does not automatically mean two families should be merged. It identifies an area requiring further clinical and architectural consideration.

measure_descriptions.discriminators: How much of the two families' symptom-discriminator vocabulary is the same, on a 0 to 1 scale. 0 means nothing in common, 1 means identical.
measure_descriptions.questions: How much of the two families' question sets is the same, on a 0 to 1 scale.
measure_descriptions.snomed: How much of the two families' SNOMED concept sets is the same, on a 0 to 1 scale. SNOMED coverage in this dataset is sparse, so this is the thinnest of the three similarity measures.
measure_descriptions.transitions: How many recorded handover instructions run between the two families, in either direction. The most directly understandable measure: it counts something the data records rather than a calculated similarity.

association.explanation: The best-matching family is well ahead of the next best, so the pathway's placement is clear from its structure.
association.label: Clearly belongs to one family

association.explanation: A second family is a reasonable match, so the placement depends on judgement.
association.label: Somewhat ambiguous

association.explanation: Two or more families match almost equally well. Structure alone cannot place these pathways.
association.label: Highly ambiguous

routing.optimistic_bound_note: These figures are measured with the whole pathway known. A live system would have to decide from partial answers, which is harder, so treat this as the best case rather than the expected case.
routing.why_it_matters: If separate models were used, something would have to decide which model handles an incoming case. This measures how far that decision can be made from structure alone. It does not design that mechanism, which is Phase 3 work.

definitions.duplication_if_separated: If every family held its own copy of each shared feature, this is how many extra copies would exist. It is a count of duplication in the structure, not an estimate of size, memory or cost.

shared_core.interpretation_note: This does not conclude that a separate shared model is required. A feature used everywhere might be one clinical concept genuinely used everywhere, several different concepts that happen to share wording, or a by-product of how the pathways were written. Structure alone cannot tell those apart.

split_candidates.mechanical_caveat: Dividing a family always reduces the share of handovers that stay inside each part, because handovers that used to be internal now cross a boundary. As with merges, the measure that carries real information is clinical similarity.
split_candidates.no_recommendation_note: No split is proposed. These are before-and-after measurements for review.

tells_us.text: 14 different ways of grouping the estate were tested. The set presented here holds 34 candidate families, the largest containing 123 pathways and the typical one 7.
tells_us.title: Repeatable candidate groupings emerge from the data

tells_us.text: Several clustering methods were run separately. Their agreement ranges from 0.04 to 0.75 on a 0 to 1 scale, which means the grouping reflects the data rather than one algorithm's assumptions.
tells_us.title: Independent methods broadly agree on the structure

tells_us.text: 26 of 34 families had no dominant symptom group or clinical area, so they were deliberately left unnamed rather than given a clinical-sounding label the evidence does not support.
tells_us.title: Most candidate families do not match an existing NHS grouping

tells_us.text: 63% of pathways hand over to a pathway outside their own family, and 55 connect several families at once.
tells_us.title: Boundaries between families are real but busy

tells_us.text: 424 features appear across many candidate families. Separating the families entirely would mean 2,735 duplicate copies of that content.
tells_us.title: Some content would have to be shared or duplicated

tells_us.text: 47% of pathways clearly belong to one family on structural evidence; 22% could sit in two or more equally well.
tells_us.title: Placement is clear for some pathways and not others
